reasoning:
Both submissions make the identical executable change, and it is the right one. At the TT probe site, `cp (hl)` computes entDepth - curDepth, so CF=1 exactly when the stored entry is shallower than the current search. The shipped code guarded with `jr z,ttNoCut`, which refuses a cutoff only on an exact depth match and therefore happily cuts on entries that are too shallow — precisely the reported symptom: iterative deepening stores the level-2 result, and every deeper iteration probes it, takes the cutoff, and propagates the depth-2 move and score to the root while still burning the clock walking the tree. Both authors replace it with `jr c,ttNoCut`, which rejects only the shallow-entry case and restores the documented "usable only if entry depth >= current depth" rule. Both also implicitly change the equal-depth case from "never cut" to "cut", which is the correct semantics rather than a regression, and both share whatever residual exposure exists around a depth-0 empty slot probed at curDepth 0 — identical code, identical risk, so correctness_risk is genuinely tied at 5. Nothing else in the reported behaviour (movegen/perft, rendering, legality, mate detection) is touched by either.

The submissions diverge on scope and presentation. X confines itself to the two lines at the fault, annotating the flag semantics (`CF set <=> entDepth < curDepth`) and, usefully, the consequence of falling through: "shallower entry: keep its move, reject the bound" — which tells a reviewer why the label is `ttNoCut` and not `ttSkip`, i.e. that the stale entry is still worth its move for ordering. That is the smallest change that fixes the defect and it explains itself completely.

Y makes the same one-instruction fix with a three-line block comment that is also correct and is slightly more explicit that entDepth < curDepth is the *only* case that must not cut (a helpful justification for why `jr z` was wrong). But Y additionally rewrites an unrelated block of the file header ~230 lines away, restating the 48K table as 4 KB / 512 buckets at TT_BASE = 0xC000 with a 9-bit key mask and a 0x1000-byte clear, in place of 8 KB / 1024 buckets at 0x6000. That edit is pure comment, so it cannot break the build, but it has nothing to do with the depth comparison; it is internally self-consistent (8 bytes/bucket either way) yet unverifiable from the diff, so a reviewer either takes it on faith or goes and re-derives the whole addressing scheme to approve a one-byte opcode change. That is the definition of unwarranted scope on this rubric, and it is why Y loses on minimality (3) and, marginally, on clarity (4) — the fix comment is also somewhat redundant with the existing line it sits beneath, and it omits the fall-through insight X captures.

Since the functional fixes are equivalent, the tiebreak is entirely scope and reviewability, and X wins on both. Merge X; if the header geometry really is stale, that belongs in a separate documentation commit where it can be checked against ttAddr/ttClear on its own merits. Blinding note: nothing in either diff prompted a theory about authorship or process; the scores reflect the code and comments only.
